claim: Contamination with exogenous DNA is a constant hazard to ancient DNA studies, since their validity greatly depend on the ancient origin of the retrieved sequences.
source: Contamination with exogenous DNA is a constant hazard to ancient DNA studies, since their validity greatly depend on the ancient origin of the retrieved sequences.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about ancient DNA research challenges.

claim: It is fundamental to show positive evidence for the authenticity of ancient DNA sequences even when preventive measures to avoid contamination are implemented.
source: Since contamination occurs sporadically, it is fundamental to show positive evidence for the authenticity of ancient DNA sequences even when preventive measures to avoid contamination are implemented.
evidence: This is a methodological principle based on established scientific knowledge about ancient DNA authentication requirements.

claim: The presence of wheat in the United Kingdom 8000 years before the present has been reported based on an analysis of sedimentary ancient DNA.
source: Recently the presence of wheat in the United Kingdom 8000 years before the present has been reported based on an analysis of sedimentary ancient DNA (Smith et al. 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Smith et al. 2015.

claim: Smith et al. did not present any positive evidence for the authenticity of their results due to the small number of sequencing reads that were confidently assigned to wheat.
source: Smith et al. did not present any positive evidence for the authenticity of their results due to the small number of sequencing reads that were confidently assigned to wheat.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' analysis of the Smith et al. study.

claim: The putative wheat DNA reads are most likely not of ancient origin.
source: We applied this test to the putative wheat DNA and find that these reads are most likely not of ancient origin.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational analysis and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A vast proportion of flora and fauna do not fossilize.
source: Although a vast proportion of flora and fauna do not fossilize, traces of their DNA may be preserved in sediments allowing the characterization of past biodiversity (Pedersen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about fossilization, supported by citation.

claim: Traces of DNA from flora and fauna may be preserved in sediments allowing the characterization of past biodiversity.
source: Although a vast proportion of flora and fauna do not fossilize, traces of their DNA may be preserved in sediments allowing the characterization of past biodiversity (Pedersen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pedersen et al., 2015.

claim: Special sample preparation procedures have been developed to reduce DNA contamination.
source: Therefore, special sample preparation procedures have been developed to reduce DNA contamination (Cooper and Poinar, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cooper and Poinar, 2000.

claim: It remains difficult to estimate how well preventive measures work against DNA contamination.
source: Nevertheless, it remains difficult to estimate how well preventive measures work.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about limitations in ancient DNA research.

claim: If contamination is a possible explanation for the result, it is crucial to exclude this possibility by giving positive evidence for the authenticity of aDNA.
source: If contamination is a possible explanation for the result, it is crucial to exclude this possibility by giving positive evidence for the authenticity of aDNA (Prüfer and Meyer, 2015).
evidence: This methodological principle is supported by citation to Prüfer and Meyer, 2015.

claim: Next generation sequencing allows for the generation of a large number of full-length DNA sequences, which allows for the authentication of aDNA.
source: Fortunately, a large number of full-length DNA sequences can be generated using next generation sequencing, which allows for the authentication of aDNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about next generation sequencing capabilities.

claim: In aDNA an excess of C-to-T (cytosine to thymine) substitutions occur at the 5′ and 3′ ends of molecules.
source: In aDNA an excess of C-to-T (cytosine to thymine) substitutions occur at the 5′ and 3′ ends of molecules (or its mirror image G-to-A (guanine to adenine) at the 3′ end, depending on the library protocol employed).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ancient DNA damage patterns.

claim: When considering the 5′ end of sequences, the excess of C-to-T substitutions is highest at the first base and decreases exponentially towards the center.
source: When considering the 5′ end of sequences, the excess of C-to-T substitutions is highest at the first base and decreases exponentially towards the center (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A showing the pattern.

claim: The pattern of C-to-T substitutions is the result of cytosine deamination to uracil in single stranded overhangs.
source: This pattern is the result of cytosine deamination to uracil in single stranded overhangs (Briggs et al., 2007).
evidence: This mechanistic explanation is supported by citation to Briggs et al., 2007.

claim: The C-to-T substitution pattern is present in aDNA-derived sequences but absent in much younger samples.
source: Since it is present in aDNA-derived sequences but absent in much younger samples, it has been used as an authentication criterion in aDNA experiments (Krause et al., 2010; Prüfer and Meyer, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Krause et al., 2010 and Prüfer and Meyer, 2015.

claim: The C-to-T substitution pattern has been used as an authentication criterion in aDNA experiments.
source: Since it is present in aDNA-derived sequences but absent in much younger samples, it has been used as an authentication criterion in aDNA experiments (Krause et al., 2010; Prüfer and Meyer, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krause et al., 2010 and Prüfer and Meyer, 2015.

claim: Smith et al. analyzed sediments from Bouldnor Cliff, a submerged archeological site in the United Kingdom.
source: Smith et al. analyzed sediments from Bouldnor Cliff, a submerged archeological site in the United Kingdom, and suggested the presence of domesticated wheat 8000 years ago based on sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the Smith et al. study.

claim: Smith et al. suggested the presence of domesticated wheat 8000 years ago based on sedimentary ancient DNA.
source: Smith et al. analyzed sediments from Bouldnor Cliff, a submerged archeological site in the United Kingdom, and suggested the presence of domesticated wheat 8000 years ago based on sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the Smith et al. study's conclusion.

claim: The presence of wheat 8000 years ago is 2000 years earlier than expected based on archeological remains in the British Isles.
source: This is 2000 years earlier than expected based on archeological remains in the British Isles and 400 years earlier than in nearby European sites (reviewed in Smith et al.).
evidence: This claim is based on information reviewed in Smith et al.

claim: The presence of wheat 8000 years ago is 400 years earlier than in nearby European sites.
source: This is 2000 years earlier than expected based on archeological remains in the British Isles and 400 years earlier than in nearby European sites (reviewed in Smith et al.).
evidence: This claim is based on information reviewed in Smith et al.

claim: Smith et al. did not find wheat pollen or archeological remains associated with wheat cultivation.
source: Since Smith et al. did not find wheat pollen or archeological remains associated with wheat cultivation, they conclude that the wheat presence in Bouldnor Cliff was the result of trading.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the Smith et al. study findings.

claim: Smith et al. conclude that the wheat presence in Bouldnor Cliff was the result of trading.
source: Since Smith et al. did not find wheat pollen or archeological remains associated with wheat cultivation, they conclude that the wheat presence in Bouldnor Cliff was the result of trading.
evidence: This is a statement about the conclusion drawn by Smith et al.

claim: Smith et al. produced approximately 72 million Illumina reads in total.
source: In total they produced ∼72 million Illumina reads, of which they robustly assigned 152 to wheat (Triticum), with dozens more (160 reads) to higher taxonomic ranks that include wheat.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the Smith et al. study data.

claim: Smith et al. robustly assigned 152 reads to wheat (Triticum).
source: In total they produced ∼72 million Illumina reads, of which they robustly assigned 152 to wheat (Triticum), with dozens more (160 reads) to higher taxonomic ranks that include wheat.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the Smith et al. study results.

claim: Smith et al. assigned 160 reads to higher taxonomic ranks that include wheat.
source: In total they produced ∼72 million Illumina reads, of which they robustly assigned 152 to wheat (Triticum), with dozens more (160 reads) to higher taxonomic ranks that include wheat.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the Smith et al. study results.

claim: Smith et al. took state-of-the art preventive measures to avoid contamination.
source: Smith et al. took state-of-the art preventive measures to avoid contamination and exercised great effort to ensure the accuracy and robustness of their phylogenetic assignments.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the Smith et al. study methodology.

claim: Smith et al. exercised great effort to ensure the accuracy and robustness of their phylogenetic assignments.
source: Smith et al. took state-of-the art preventive measures to avoid contamination and exercised great effort to ensure the accuracy and robustness of their phylogenetic assignments.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the Smith et al. study methodology.

claim: Smith et al. attempted to authenticate the aDNA molecules based on the expected excess of C-to-T substitutions.
source: The authors attempted to authenticate the aDNA molecules based on the expected excess of C-to-T substitutions, but because of the very small number of reads assigned to wheat, they failed to do so using standard approaches.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the Smith et al. study methodology.

claim: Smith et al. failed to authenticate the aDNA molecules using standard approaches because of the very small number of reads assigned to wheat.
source: The authors attempted to authenticate the aDNA molecules based on the expected excess of C-to-T substitutions, but because of the very small number of reads assigned to wheat, they failed to do so using standard approaches.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the Smith et al. study results.

claim: The excess of C-to-T substitutions at the 5′ end occurs at different magnitudes in samples of different ages.
source: Although the excess of C-to-T substitutions at the 5′ end occurs at different magnitudes in samples of different ages, the exponential increase of substitutions towards the end is a ubiquitous pattern in aDNA studies (Sawyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Sawyer et al., 2012.

claim: The exponential increase of substitutions towards the end is a ubiquitous pattern in aDNA studies.
source: Although the excess of C-to-T substitutions at the 5′ end occurs at different magnitudes in samples of different ages, the exponential increase of substitutions towards the end is a ubiquitous pattern in aDNA studies (Sawyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Sawyer et al., 2012.

claim: True aDNA libraries show significant goodness-of-fit p-values for exponential decay of C-to-T substitutions.
source: As expected, true aDNA libraries show significant goodness-of-fit p-values (Figure 1A), whereas non-significant goodness-of-fit p-values, neither decay nor growth, are observed in libraries derived from modern DNA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Non-significant goodness-of-fit p-values, neither decay nor growth, are observed in libraries derived from modern DNA.
source: As expected, true aDNA libraries show significant goodness-of-fit p-values (Figure 1A), whereas non-significant goodness-of-fit p-values, neither decay nor growth, are observed in libraries derived from modern DNA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A significant goodness-of-fit p-value indicates C-to-T exponential decay at the 5′ end.
source: A given C-to-T damage pattern plot can thus be summarized by its goodness-of-fit p-value that when it is significant indicates C-to-T exponential decay at the 5′ end (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological inference supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: 10,000 sets of 150 sequences were resampled (with replacement) from a library of historic Solanum tuberosum collected in 1846.
source: We resampled (with replacement) 10,000 sets of 150 sequences from a library of historic Solanum tuberosum collected in 1846 (Yoshida et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in the study, with citation.

claim: The number 150 was selected to be comparable to the 152 reads that Smith et al. assigned to wheat.
source: The number was selected to be comparable to the 152 reads that Smith et al. assigned to wheat.
evidence: This is an explanation of the methodological choice.

claim: The sedaDNA goodness-of-fit p-value falls within the upper 3% of subsamples with the least good fit when compared to historic S. tuberosum.
source: When we evaluate the sedaDNA goodness-of-fit p-value, we find that it falls within the upper 3% of subsamples with the least good fit.
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis performed in the study.

claim: The null hypothesis that the sequences assigned to wheat are as ancient as the historic S. tuberosum library can be rejected.
source: We can therefore reject the null hypothesis that the sequences assigned to wheat are as ancient as the historic S. tuberosum library.
evidence: This is a statistical inference based on the data analysis.

claim: When compared to a modern wheat library, the sedaDNA shows a better match (p = 0.83).
source: We repeated the whole procedure using this time a modern wheat library to generate the distribution of goodness-of-fit p-values (Figure 2A) and find a better match (p = 0.83).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The hypothesis that the sequences assigned to wheat are of modern origin cannot be rejected.
source: Thus, we cannot reject the hypothesis that the sequences assigned to wheat are of modern origin.
evidence: This is a statistical inference based on the data analysis.

claim: A set of samples from animal and plant remains with an age of 85–170 years before present was used to investigate how the test behaves with different aDNA libraries.
source: For this purpose we used a set of samples from animal (Sawyer et al., 2012) and plant remains (Yoshida et al., 2013) with an age of 85–170 years before present, and scored the sedaDNA wheat sequences against distributions generated from these libraries (subsamples of 150 sequences again).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology with citations.

claim: The goodness-of-fit p-value for the libraries is positively correlated with the empirical p-value for the sedaDNA wheat sequences tested against them.
source: We observed that the goodness-of-fit p-value for the libraries is positively correlated with the empirical p-value for the sedaDNA wheat sequences tested against them (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Using a significance level of 0.05, the hypothesis that the wheat sequences are of ancient origin was rejected with 7 out of 13 libraries used in the test.
source: Using a significance level of 0.05, we rejected the hypothesis that the wheat sequences are of ancient origin with 7 out of 13 libraries used in our test (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The purportedly 8000-year old wheat sequences show a less pronounced deamination pattern than many plant and animal samples with an age of less of 200 years.
source: Thus, the purportedly 8000-year old wheat sequences show a less pronounced deamination pattern than many plant and animal samples with an age of less of 200 years.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative analysis of deamination patterns.

claim: A 7000-years-old human Mesolithic sample from la Braña site in Northern Iberia was used to score the sedaDNA.
source: Finally, we took a less conservative approach and scored the sedaDNA against a distribution of goodness-of-fit p-values (subsamples of 150 read) generated from a 7000-years-old human Mesolithic sample from la Braña site in Northern Iberia (Olalde et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology with citation.

claim: La Braña is a site with cold environment and stable thermal conditions that has yielded exceptionally well conserved human fossils with approximately 50% of human endogenous DNA.
source: La Braña is a site with cold environment and stable thermal conditions that has yielded exceptionally well conserved human fossils with ∼50% of human endogenous DNA that reach a ∼15% C-to-T substitution rate at the 5′ end (Olalde et al., 2014a) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is information supported by citation to Olalde et al., 2014a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The la Braña sample reaches approximately 15% C-to-T substitution rate at the 5′ end.
source: La Braña is a site with cold environment and stable thermal conditions that has yielded exceptionally well conserved human fossils with ∼50% of human endogenous DNA that reach a ∼15% C-to-T substitution rate at the 5′ end (Olalde et al., 2014a) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is data supported by citation to Olalde et al., 2014a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The null hypothesis that the sedaDNA reads are as ancient as the sample from la Braña can be rejected (p = 0.0014).
source: We could reject the null hypothesis that the sedaDNA reads are as ancient as the sample from la Braña (p = 0.0014), a sample that is closer in time with the allegedly 8000-year-old wheat reads (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Almost all 10,000 subsamples from la Braña had a very low (close to 0) goodness-of-fit p-value, even though only 150 reads were subsampled.
source: It is worth pointing out that almost all 10,000 subsamples from la Braña had a very low (close to 0) goodness-of-fit p-value, even though we subsample only 150 reads (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The hypothesis that a true aDNA library is ancient was never rejected in the statistical power assessment.
source: Whereas the hypothesis that a true aDNA library is ancient was never rejected (Figure 3A), the hypothesis that a modern library has ancient origin could be rejected only when sufficient number of sequences were used for the subsample test (in tests with more than 300 reads the median empirical p-value was always below 0.05) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical power analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The hypothesis that a modern library has ancient origin could be rejected only when sufficient number of sequences were used for the subsample test.
source: Whereas the hypothesis that a true aDNA library is ancient was never rejected (Figure 3A), the hypothesis that a modern library has ancient origin could be rejected only when sufficient number of sequences were used for the subsample test (in tests with more than 300 reads the median empirical p-value was always below 0.05) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical power analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In tests with more than 300 reads the median empirical p-value was always below 0.05 for modern DNA libraries.
source: Whereas the hypothesis that a true aDNA library is ancient was never rejected (Figure 3A), the hypothesis that a modern library has ancient origin could be rejected only when sufficient number of sequences were used for the subsample test (in tests with more than 300 reads the median empirical p-value was always below 0.05) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical power analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All reads sequenced by Smith et al. were mapped to the wheat genome after skipping the phylogenetic curation step.
source: Finally, we skipped the phylogenetic curation step applied by Smith et al. to reduce the number of false positive wheat alignments, and mapped all reads sequenced by Smith et al. to the wheat genome.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in the study.

claim: The empirical p-value was dependent on the number of reads tested, and declined with an increasing number of tested reads for all layers of sediments sequenced in Smith et al.
source: The empirical p-value was dependent on the number of reads tested, and declined with an increasing number of tested reads for all layers of sediments sequenced in Smith et al (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The pattern of declining empirical p-value with increasing reads resembled the one obtained from a modern DNA library.
source: This pattern resembled the one obtained from a modern DNA library (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a comparative inference based on data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The hypothesis that the mapped reads are of ancient origin can be rejected (mean p-value < 0.05 for all tests with more than 400 reads for layers 1–2 and 4, and 800 reads for layer 3).
source: As for the phylogenetic curated 152 sequences, we were able to reject the hypothesis that the mapped reads are of ancient origin (mean p-value < 0.05 for all tests with more than 400 reads for layers 1–2 and 4, and 800 reads for layer 3).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis.

claim: The 152 sequences after phylogenetic curation are not a biased subsample from the distribution of all wheat-matching sequences.
source: Our analysis also shows that the 152 sequences after phylogenetic curation are not a biased subsample from the distribution of all wheat-matching sequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative analysis.

claim: The hypothesis that the sequences assigned to wheat by Smith et al. are of ancient origin can be rejected.
source: We were able to reject the hypothesis that the sequences assigned to wheat by Smith et al. are of ancient origin.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on the data analysis.

claim: The rejection of ancient origin holds true even when comparing the putative 8000 year old sequences with only century old samples that show much lower deamination signatures.
source: This is true even when we compared the putative 8000 year old sequences with only century old samples that show much lower deamination signatures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative analysis with different aged samples.

claim: A scenario in which wheat was transported to the Bouldnor Cliff site 8000 years ago is unwarranted.
source: This means that a scenario in which wheat was transported to the Bouldnor Cliff site 8000 years ago is unwarranted.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the inference from the data analysis.

claim: The approach for authentication of aDNA can be used even with a very small number of sequences.
source: Our approach for authentication of aDNA can be used even with a very small number of sequences, and we hope that it will proof useful to test for positive evidence of authenticity for ancient DNA studies whose conclusions rely heavily on the ancient origin of the analyzed sequences.
evidence: This is a claim about the utility of the method based on the demonstrated analysis.

claim: The computational method compares postmortem damage patterns of a test dataset with bona fide ancient and modern DNA.
source: We developed a computational method that compares postmortem damage patterns of a test dataset with bona fide ancient and modern DNA.
evidence: This is a description of the method developed in the study.

claim: An exponential function was fitted to the frequency of C-to-T substitutions for the first 20 nucleotides at the 5′ end.
source: We fitted an exponential function to the frequency of C-to-T substitutions for the first 20 nucleotides at the 5′ end.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology.

claim: The fitting was carried out with the model formula: y ∼ N∗exp(−rate∗x).
source: The fitting was carried out with the model formula: y ∼ N∗exp(−rate∗x).
evidence: This is a description of the mathematical model used.

claim: A goodness-of-fit p-value was calculated by using a one-sided t-test from the nls fitting.
source: From the nls fitting we obtained the t-value and degrees of freedom for the rate parameter and then calculated a goodness-of-fit p-value by using a one-sided t-test.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methodology.
